extracted.intended_audience: state and tribal agencies, environmental attorneys, EPA rulewriters, and public commenters on the proposed §401 rule
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/public-comment guidance evaluating EPA's proposed revisions to Clean Water Act §401, focusing on statutory interpretation, procedural rules, burden of proof, scope of state authority, information requirements, and timing for certification requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'applicant' in §401(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposes to interpret the use of the term 'applicant' in section 401(d) as identifying the person or entity responsible for obtaining and complying with the certification. The term 'applicant' is plain and unambiguous, and neither PUD No. 1 nor other authority suggests a contrary interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must explain how its interpretation of 'applicant' entails limiting 401(d) to conditions on that applicant's discharges, and how interpreting 401(a)(1) and 401(d) as coextensive gives effect to Congress’s choice to use different words ('discharge' vs 'applicant'). Absent such explanation, reaffirming the established understanding is required. Brand X does not supply authority to overturn a plain-text step-1 decision without showing reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Other appropriate requirement of state law" scope
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA suggests this phrase should cover only EPA-approved CWA regulatory programs that control discharges, but states retain authority under 401(d) (and via §301 referencing §303) to impose broader non-discharge-based limits necessary to protect water quality standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if 'other appropriate requirement' were read narrowly, independent authority rooted in §301 and §303 permits states to impose non-discharge conditions (e.g., in‑stream flow conditions upheld in PUD No. 1). EPA cannot rely on a narrow reading of 'other appropriate requirement' to justify limiting state authority under §401(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand X cannot justify overturning PUD No. 1 here
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cites National Cable & Telecommunications Ass'n v. Brand X to reject PUD No. 1's interpretation, but PUD No. 1 did not choose among competing reasonable interpretations of ambiguous text; it was effectively a Chevron step 1/plain-meaning decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brand X applies only where reasonable ambiguity exists and a later agency interpretation fills that gap; EPA must show §401's language is ambiguous and that its interpretation is reasonable—neither has been done.

rubrics_metrics.name: §401 is not limited to point-source discharges
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court (S.D. Warren) found the plain meaning of 'discharge' to be a 'flowing or issuing out.' The statutory structure differentiates 'discharge' (broad) from 'discharge of a pollutant' (point-source addition), indicating Congress did not intend 'discharge' to be limited to point sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cannot rewrite §401 to add a point‑source limitation that Congress omitted. Courts (e.g., AES Sparrows Point) have applied the broader 'flowing or issuing out' meaning to non-point activities. Canon of statutory construction (Russello/Barnhart/Conn. Nat’l Bank) supports reading 'discharge' broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency may not insert omitted statutory language
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not at liberty to add language (e.g., 'point source') into §401 that Congress chose not to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory-construction canons require respecting Congress's distinct word choices; EPA must not impose qualifications absent in the text or a clear congressional mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for certification denials
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 401 requires an affirmative showing that the discharge will comply with applicable provisions; the statute places the burden on the applicant and permits the certifying authority to certify only if it can conclude the project will comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed §121.5(e) improperly reverses the burden by requiring states to identify requirements the project 'will not comply' with and to justify why compliance is unachievable. The rule should instead require states to identify 'the specific water quality requirements that the state cannot confirm the proposed project will comply with' and explain why the state cannot confirm compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to deny based on insufficient information or unacceptable risk
rubrics_metrics.description: States may deny certification when applicants fail to provide complete information or when residual risks (e.g., frac-outs, tailings dam failures) are unacceptably likely even if a violation is not certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States should be permitted to deny on precautionary grounds; they should explain the risks of concern and how potential incidents would violate water quality requirements. The Proposed Rule must not constrain denials to only cases where a violation is certain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal permitting agencies lack authority to review substance of state 401 decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 401(a)(1) and 401(d) give the state decision controlling effect ('no license or permit shall be granted' if state denies; state conditions 'shall become a condition on any Federal license or permit'). EPA's proposals to allow federal agencies to treat state denials as waivers or to strip or replace state-imposed conditions are unsupported by the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every Circuit to consider the matter has held federal permitting agencies lack authority to review the substantive merits of state 401 decisions. The only correct remedy for alleged improper state denials/conditions is judicial review; EPA cannot create a parallel federal substantive review or veto process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal agency review limited to procedural compliance, not substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal permitting agencies may verify compliance with explicit procedural requirements of §401 (e.g., whether the proper state acted, timing), but they may not resolve substantive disputes about state-law procedures or substitute their judgment for state substantive determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like City of Tacoma limit federal agency inquiries to procedural verification and caution agencies not to 'second guess' or construe state law. Federal agencies also lack authority to add legal requirements not present in the statute or state law (e.g., claim preclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA cannot limit §401 to EPA‑approved water quality requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposes defining 'water quality requirements' narrowly (effluent limitations, WQ-related effluent limitations, water quality standards, national performance standards, toxic/pretreatment effluent standards, and EPA-approved state/tribal CWA program provisions), but that undermines the broad state authority Congress intended and lacks textual support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Congress intended such an enumerated scope it could have done so; EPA's selective legislative-history citation does not support requiring EPA approval of state requirements. EPA must explain and justify any narrowing with evidence; its anecdotal claims about irrelevant conditions lack context and detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: clock starts only on a valid certification request
rubrics_metrics.description: While some courts have allowed the §401 clock to run from receipt of any application, the better reading (and some courts) require a 'valid' request before triggering the one-year waiver period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposed list of documents to constitute a 'certification request' is a reasonable start but falls short; the agency should require minimum substantive information so the state/tribe can meaningfully begin review (see the minimum-contents criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum contents of a valid certification request
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid 'certification request' must include far more than 'location and type of any discharge' and 'location of receiving water.' At minimum it should contain: designations of affected waterways (including impairment status and high/exceptional quality), specific description of the type(s) of discharge (chemical composition, thermal/non-chemical discharges), source of discharge, estimated volume of each discharge, identification of the number of discharges into each waterway and watershed, an estimated date for applicant to provide direct/indirect/cumulative impacts analysis, identification of any other water-quality impacts, an estimated date for a complete mitigation plan with site-specific mitigation details, payment of applicable fees, documentation or a statement regarding prior contamination, and certification that the federal agency was notified the same day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should: (1) revise Item 4 to include sub‑items (designation, impairment status, high/exceptional quality, chemical/thermal composition, source, volume, number of discharges, cumulative impacts analysis date, other impacts); (2) require mitigation-plan delivery dates; (3) include fee payment in the definition of 'certification request'; (4) require documentation about prior contamination; (5) provide a process for states to notify federal agencies that an initial submission is deficient; and (6) require same‑day notice to the relevant federal agency with transmission method and contact name. A single standard form is unlikely to be sufficient for all projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA cannot arbitrarily shorten the 'reasonable time' or force waivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress provided a 'reasonable period of time (which shall not exceed one year)' to prevent undue delay, not to set timelines that make certification impossible. EPA cannot set deadlines that deprive states/tribes of substantive authority or lead to premature waivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While federal agencies may adopt regulations defining 'reasonable time,' they lack unfettered discretion to impose deadlines that prevent states from exercising their §401 authority. Evidence suggests applicant omissions, not state delay, cause most processing delays. EPA's rule should not permit federal agencies to find waiver prematurely or to adopt arbitrarily short deadlines without state/tribal input or recourse.
